headline: Nylas Agent Accounts enable two-way appointment reminders that can reschedule automatically
summary: This new system allows applications to own their own mailboxes and calendars, automating replies and rescheduling without human intervention.
details: Traditional appointment reminder systems are often one-way, leading to missed reschedule requests when patients reply. The new Agent Account system by Nylas addresses this by enabling automated, two-way communication.

An Agent Account is a dedicated mailbox and calendar for an application, allowing it to send reminders, receive replies, and act on reschedule requests autonomously. It operates with its own email address, like reminders@clinic.yourapp.nylas.email.

The system uses Nylas API endpoints, allowing the agent to update its own calendar events and send updated invites directly to patients. This eliminates the need for human triage of routine rescheduling requests.

Developers can integrate this functionality using the Nylas CLI or direct API calls. The core mechanism involves the agent owning the calendar event, with replies processed via webhooks to drive rescheduling logic.

A key component is the grant_id received after creating an Agent Account, which provides immediate access to the agent's mailbox and calendar without OAuth or refresh tokens. This simplifies API interactions for developers.

While powerful, users are reminded that this is a demo walkthrough, not a compliance blueprint. Handling patient data (PHI) requires careful consideration of security, retention, and BAA questions with a dedicated security team.

headline_marked: [[Period tracker Stardust shared sensitive health data]] with third parties, audit reveals
headline: Period tracker Stardust shared sensitive health data with third parties, audit reveals
summary: An audit by Mozilla Foundation and Harvard found Stardust, an astrology-themed period tracker, sent users' reproductive health details to an unlisted data firm, scoring 2 out of 10 for privacy.
details: The astrology-themed period tracker Stardust was found to send users' reproductive health details, including birth control type, pregnancy status, moods, and specific symptoms, to a data firm not named in its privacy policy. This concerning revelation came from a Mozilla Foundation audit conducted in partnership with Harvard's Berkman Klein Center.

Stardust received a score of 2 out of 10 for privacy, making it the worst performer among the six popular trackers evaluated in the audit. Mozilla researcher Shoshana Wodinsky discovered that the app begins pinging third-party trackers from the moment it opens, even before a user enters any personal information.

Upon logging a symptom, details were immediately sent to the analytics firm RudderStack, accompanied by a persistent user ID, with no in-app option to disable this sharing. Furthermore, Stardust provides Facebook with an ad identifier, linking users' in-app behavior to their existing profiles on the platform.

In stark contrast, Euki, a nonprofit-run period tracker, achieved a perfect score of 10 out of 10 for privacy. It requires no account, ensures health data never leaves the user's phone, and offers robust features like PIN protection, automatic data deletion, and a decoy screen for enhanced security.
